title: Solutions Lab 4 practice
text:
For importing, use the read_xlsx()function and specify the sheet argument.

library(readxl)
library(tidyverse)

# declare where you are in your project folder
i_am("practice1.R")

# construct the path to your data
path <- here("data", "ecommerce.xlsx")

# read the two sheets by specifying the "sheet" argument
purchases <- read_xlsx(path = path, sheet = "purchases_history")
products  <- read_xlsx(path = path, sheet = "products")




library(janitor)

purchases <- purchases |> clean_names()
products <- products |> clean_names()

To compute the total number of sales by product we can use the group_by() + summarise() combo.

purchases |> 
    group_by(product) |> 
    summarise(
        number_of_sales = n()
    )

# A tibble: 7 × 2
  product      number_of_sales
  <chr>                  <int>
1 e-reader                  96
2 earphones                115
3 laptop_1                  48
4 laptop_2                  46
5 smartphone_1              49
6 smartphone_2              52
7 tablet                    94


There is even a faster way to count how many times the values of a given variable appear in the dataset. Literally, you can pipe the count() function

purchases |> 
    count(product)

# A tibble: 7 × 2
  product          n
  <chr>        <int>
1 e-reader        96
2 earphones      115
3 laptop_1        48
4 laptop_2        46
5 smartphone_1    49
6 smartphone_2    52
7 tablet          94





To compute the total amount of money spent on each product we first join the two datasets,

purchases |> 
    left_join(products, by = "product") 

# A tibble: 500 × 3
   customer_id                          product      price_euro
   <chr>                                <chr>             <dbl>
 1 7c57e656-e132-4090-a42c-af3da335f983 earphones          90.0
 2 51f62c14-5fab-48b2-b3db-83f6c270153b smartphone_1      500. 
 3 447afb33-d3a9-4b47-bb28-22afeca71956 e-reader          200. 
 4 7a75918d-6afe-4fcf-90ff-ef0f975ad4b3 laptop_2          900. 
 5 7e6a33e0-a3d9-4414-9ce5-54865234cc88 laptop_1         2140. 
 6 1fb2ad31-4e09-4666-a379-d43b4dedc772 tablet            520. 
 7 49a97785-ab6f-470b-99ec-637b88d8c55d e-reader          200. 
 8 bd93547a-c9f1-4976-bca2-8cad699ab311 laptop_2          900. 
 9 b07a4ce7-8277-4d0c-81a4-d60ca7ba2ba6 e-reader          200. 
10 9f69d7ef-9842-476c-b403-40d599253c56 e-reader          200. 
# ℹ 490 more rows


and then comput the totals,

purchases |> 
    left_join(products, by = "product") |> 
    group_by(product) |> 
    summarise(
        total = sum(price_euro),
        total_thousands = sum(price_euro)/1000
        )

# A tibble: 7 × 3
  product        total total_thousands
  <chr>          <dbl>           <dbl>
1 e-reader      19199.            19.2
2 earphones     10349.            10.3
3 laptop_1     102720.           103. 
4 laptop_2      41400.            41.4
5 smartphone_1  24500.            24.5
6 smartphone_2  15599.            15.6
7 tablet        48879.            48.9


Equivalently, we can also first count how many items have been sold by product type, as in the previous exercise, and then join the resulting table with the price listings

purchases |> 
    count(product) |> 
    left_join(products)

# A tibble: 7 × 3
  product          n price_euro
  <chr>        <int>      <dbl>
1 e-reader        96      200. 
2 earphones      115       90.0
3 laptop_1        48     2140. 
4 laptop_2        46      900. 
5 smartphone_1    49      500. 
6 smartphone_2    52      300. 
7 tablet          94      520. 


Once here, we need to compute total by product by multiplying their prices and quantities sold

purchases |> 
    count(product) |> 
    left_join(products) |> 
    mutate(
        total_thousands = price_euro * n /1000
    )

# A tibble: 7 × 4
  product          n price_euro total_thousands
  <chr>        <int>      <dbl>           <dbl>
1 e-reader        96      200.             19.2
2 earphones      115       90.0            10.3
3 laptop_1        48     2140.            103. 
4 laptop_2        46      900.             41.4
5 smartphone_1    49      500.             24.5
6 smartphone_2    52      300.             15.6
7 tablet          94      520.             48.9

library(readxl)

# construct the path to your data

We need to use pivot_longer() to reshape the data:

new_avo <- avocados |>

Once reshaped, we can plot the price trajectories over time:

new_avo |>

As always, we can customise the plots as we prefer:

library(ggokabeito)

title: Solutions Lab 2 practice
text:
I saved my R code in a script called practice1.R which is stored in the project folder.
First, we load all the packages that we are going to use

library(tidyverse)
library(here)
library(readxl)
library(writexl)

Then, we read the data.

# declare where you are in your project folder
i_am("practice1.R")

# construct the path to your data
path <- here("data", "employees.xlsx")

# read the data and store it in dt
dt <- read_xlsx(path=path)




The function dim() returns the dimensions of the input. The first number is the number of rows. The second denotes the number of columns.

dim(dt)

[1] 150   6


Thus, the dataset stored in dt collects information about 150 employees.
You can extract the same dimensions by using the specialised functions nrow()and ncol()

nrow(dt)

[1] 150

ncol(dt)

[1] 6


A convenient way to quickly summarise the variables in your dataset is the function summary().

summary(dt)

     last_name       first_name      department    seniority     
 Length   :150   Length   :150   Length   :150   Min.   : 0.000  
 N.unique :140   N.unique :134   N.unique :  6   1st Qu.: 4.000  
 N.blank  :  0   N.blank  :  0   N.blank  :  0   Median : 7.000  
 Min.nchar:  3   Min.nchar:  3   Min.nchar:  2   Mean   : 7.487  
 Max.nchar: 19   Max.nchar: 12   Max.nchar: 10   3rd Qu.:12.000  
                                                 Max.   :15.000  
     salary             ID      
 Min.   : 42664   Min.   :1001  
 1st Qu.: 74397   1st Qu.:1038  
 Median :102606   Median :1076  
 Mean   :103789   Mean   :1076  
 3rd Qu.:129346   3rd Qu.:1113  
 Max.   :192685   Max.   :1150  


For each variable in your dataset, it returns some summary statistics. In case of numeric values, as for seniority and salary, it provides you with mean and quantiles. You can extract the same information by using the corresponding specialised functions (recall that the $operator allows you to access a given column from a data.frame object):

mean(dt$seniority)

[1] 7.486667

median(dt$seniority)

[1] 7

quantile(dt$seniority)

  0%  25%  50%  75% 100% 
   0    4    7   12   15 







We are interested in the top 3 earners from the I.T. deprtament. The arrange() function arranges values in ascending order by default. To switch to descending order you can either ask arrange() to sort according to -salary or wrap it in the desc() function:

dt |>
    filter(department=="I.T.") |>
    arrange(-salary)

# A tibble: 25 × 6
   last_name      first_name department seniority  salary    ID
   <chr>          <chr>      <chr>          <dbl>   <dbl> <dbl>
 1 Tutt           Jerry      I.T.              15 192685.  1032
 2 Aldaz          Alexis     I.T.              15 192046.  1058
 3 Clark          Harrison   I.T.              15 190690.  1114
 4 al-El-Sayed    Muna       I.T.              14 181644.  1052
 5 Running Rabbit Alexandra  I.T.              13 172680.  1103
 6 Martinez       Leydy      I.T.              12 165690.  1138

 8 Shazier        Alea       I.T.              10 148184.  1012
 9 Sherbon        Sydney     I.T.              10 146050.  1048
10 Hamlin         Connor     I.T.               9 139380.  1057
# ℹ 15 more rows

dt |>
    filter(department=="I.T.") |>
    arrange(desc(salary))

# A tibble: 25 × 6
   last_name      first_name department seniority  salary    ID
   <chr>          <chr>      <chr>          <dbl>   <dbl> <dbl>
 1 Tutt           Jerry      I.T.              15 192685.  1032
 2 Aldaz          Alexis     I.T.              15 192046.  1058
 3 Clark          Harrison   I.T.              15 190690.  1114

If you want to focus on the top three and drop all the other employess, you might want to use the function row_number()

dt |>
    filter(department=="I.T.") |>
    arrange(desc(salary)) |>
    filter(row_number()<=3)   # after arranging, you retain only employees in the top 3 rows

# A tibble: 3 × 6
  last_name first_name department seniority  salary    ID
  <chr>     <chr>      <chr>          <dbl>   <dbl> <dbl>
1 Tutt      Jerry      I.T.              15 192685.  1032
2 Aldaz     Alexis     I.T.              15 192046.  1058
3 Clark     Harrison   I.T.              15 190690.  1114





We now want to compute the median salary of the I.T. department. There are many ways to do it. The most immediate is to use

dt |>
    group_by(department) |>
    summarise(salary=median(salary))

# A tibble: 6 × 2
  department  salary
  <chr>        <dbl>
1 Accounting  80716.
2 Finance     90454.
3 HR         110257.
4 I.T.       119080.
5 Marketing  107778.
6 Sales      106649.


which evaluates the median salary of each department, included the I.T. one. If you want to focus on the I.T department, you can use the filter() function. In this case, from a logical point of view, it is equivalent if you call filter() before or after summarise()

dt |>
    filter(department=="I.T.") |>
    group_by(department) |>
    summarise(salary=median(salary))

# A tibble: 1 × 2
  department  salary
  <chr>        <dbl>
1 I.T.       119080.

dt |>
    group_by(department) |>
    summarise(salary=median(salary)) |>
    filter(department=="I.T.")

# A tibble: 1 × 2
  department  salary
  <chr>        <dbl>
1 I.T.       119080.





The exercise asks to construct a scatterplot for salary and seniority, colored by department using the ggplot2 package, which is automatically loaded with tidyverse

salary_plot <- ggplot(dt, aes(x=seniority, y=salary, color=department))+
                    geom_point()
salary_plot








The ggplot2 package offers many options for customising your plots.
A very basic tweak you typically want to apply to your graph is to change its labels by using the labs() function

salary_plot <- salary_plot +
    labs(
        x="Seniority (years since hiring)",
        y="Salary ($)",
        color="Department:"
    )
salary_plot








The labs() function can also be used to set title and subtitle of the plot

salary_plot <- salary_plot +
    labs(
        title="Does salary increase with seniority?",
        subtitle="Department by department evaluation"
    )
salary_plot








When you compare across many groups, it might be more convenient to plot groups in separate panels. You produce such plots by using the facet_grid() or the facet_wrap() functions:

salary_plot+
    facet_grid(~department)









salary_plot <- salary_plot+
    facet_wrap(~department)
salary_plot








You can use preset themes to quickly modify the appearances of your plot. For example

salary_plot + theme_bw()









salary_plot + theme_light()









salary_plot <- salary_plot + theme_minimal()
salary_plot








You can further customise your plot by using the theme() function. See ?theme() for the full list of options available. For example

salary_plot +
    theme(
        legend.position="bottom",        # move the legend in a different position
        panel.grid.minor=element_blank() # remove minor grid lines
    )








Since we are using panels to differentiate across departments, the legend for colors is not really needed, thus, it might be sensible to remove it

salary_plot <- salary_plot +
    theme(
        legend.position="none",  # remove the legend
        panel.grid.minor=element_blank() # declutter the plot by removing minor grid lines
    )
salary_plot








You can also customise the colors of the plots. For example, you can use a customised palette by specifying colors via hex codes,

my_palette <- c(
    "Accounting" = "#F7B1AB",
    "Finance"    = "#807182",
    "HR"         = "#E3DDDD",
    "I.T"        = "#A45C3D",
    "Sales"      = "#5c3410ff",
    "Marketing"  = "#1C0221"
    )
salary_plot +
    scale_color_manual(values=my_palette)








You can use ready-to-use color palettes provided by ggplot2

salary_plot+
    scale_color_viridis_d()








You can also use color palettes provided by external packages, such as ggsci or ggokabeito

library(ggokabeito)
salary_plot <- salary_plot +
    scale_color_okabe_ito()
salary_plot








Nevertheless, there are many other possibilities of customisation. You can find a whole book in this regard in the resources page.
When you are satisfied with your plot, you can save it with the ggsave() function. See ?ggsave() for a list of the exportable formats.

# You can save it in many different formats
ggsave(salary_plot, path = here("salary_plot.jpg")) # save it in jpg format
ggsave(salary_plot, path = here("salary_plot.pdf")) # save it in pdf format
ggsave(salary_plot, path = here("salary_plot.png")) # save it in png format

# You can also customise dimensions to better fit in your documents/slides
ggsave(salary_plot, path = here("salary_plot_wide.jpg"), width=10, height = 5)
ggsave(salary_plot, path = here("salary_plot_square.jpg"), width=8,  height = 8)






dt |>
    group_by(department) |>
    summarise(
        total=sum(salary),
        average=mean(salary)
    )

# A tibble: 6 × 3
  department    total average
  <chr>         <dbl>   <dbl>
1 Accounting 1856399.  80713.
2 Finance    3004418.  93888.
3 HR         2142249. 107112.
4 I.T.       3120520. 124821.
5 Marketing  2394822. 108856.
6 Sales      3049907. 108925.







To check how many employees have just been hired across all departments we can use the filter() function

dt |>
    filter(seniority==0)

# A tibble: 11 × 6
   last_name     first_name department seniority salary    ID
   <chr>         <chr>      <chr>          <dbl>  <dbl> <dbl>
 1 al-Momin      Mu'mina    Sales              0 47359.  1009
 2 Heng          Marina     Accounting         0 42770.  1026
 3 Huynh         Alicia     Finance            0 61532.  1027
 4 Zavala        Kristina   Finance            0 61431.  1068
 5 el-Ameen      Haneef     Finance            0 58284.  1089
 6 al-Abdallah   Labeeb     Finance            0 59477.  1106
 7 Hiler         Margaret   Finance            0 60065.  1123
 8 Zheng         Brittany   I.T.               0 52634.  1126
 9 al-Jamal      Muna       Marketing          0 42664.  1128
10 Apodaca-Anaya Daniel     Marketing          0 43220.  1148
11 Novell        Lindsey    I.T.               0 43226.  1149


the command returns eleven rows, so we already know the number of new hired is 11. However, we might want to explicitely compute the exact number. In this case, we can use the n() function, which do nothing else but counting elements

dt |>
    filter(seniority==0) |>
    summarise(new_hires = n())

# A tibble: 1 × 1
  new_hires
      <int>
1        11


See, however, that while you might expect to get a number, R is returning you a 1x1 tibble. If you need the numeric format, you can use

dt |>
    filter(seniority==0) |>
    summarise(new_hires = n()) |>
    as.numeric()

[1] 11





To count the new hires by department, it is sufficient to add the specification of the grouping structure, that is

new_hires_table <- dt |>
    group_by(department) |>
    filter(seniority==0) |>
    summarise(new_hires = n())
new_hires_table

# A tibble: 5 × 2
  department new_hires
  <chr>          <int>
1 Accounting         1
2 Finance            5
3 I.T.               2
4 Marketing          2
5 Sales              1


Obviously, if you sum the new hires by department, you still get 11, as expected

sum(new_hires_table$new_hires)

[1] 11


If you want to extract the value for the I.T. department you can use filter()

new_hires_table |>
    filter(department=="I.T.")

# A tibble: 1 × 2
  department new_hires
  <chr>          <int>
1 I.T.               2


and if you want to extract the numeric value only, you can use

new_hires_table |>
    filter(department=="I.T.") |>
    select(new_hires) |>
    as.numeric()

[1] 2





We focus on employees of the Finance department with at least 8 years seniority. Thus, first we specify such conditions in the filtering function, and then we summarise the salary of the filtered rows

dt |>
    filter(department=="Finance", seniority >= 8) |>
    summarise(average_salary = mean(salary))

# A tibble: 1 × 1
  average_salary
           <dbl>
1        119800.


If you want to do it by department, and at the same time checking how many employees satisfy the seniority condition, you can use

dt |>
    filter(seniority >= 8) |>
    group_by(department) |>
    summarise(
        average_salary = mean(salary),
        number_of_employees = n()
        )

# A tibble: 6 × 3
  department average_salary number_of_employees
  <chr>               <dbl>               <int>
1 Accounting        100111.                   9
2 Finance           119800.                  15
3 HR                130238.                  11
4 I.T.              162628.                  12
5 Marketing         139627.                  12
6 Sales             136137.                  15






We need to compute the median salary, the total number of employees and the number of new hires by department. To do everything it the same summarise() call, there a small “trick” for what concerns the new hires. Recall how comparisons work in terms of logical values. If you call

dt$seniority==0

  [1] FALSE FALSE FALSE FALSE FALSE FALSE FALSE FALSE  TRUE FALSE FALSE FALSE
 [13] FALSE FALSE FALSE FALSE FALSE FALSE FALSE FALSE FALSE FALSE FALSE FALSE
 [25] FALSE  TRUE  TRUE FALSE FALSE FALSE FALSE FALSE FALSE FALSE FALSE FALSE
 [37] FALSE FALSE FALSE FALSE FALSE FALSE FALSE FALSE FALSE FALSE FALSE FALSE
 [49] FALSE FALSE FALSE FALSE FALSE FALSE FALSE FALSE FALSE FALSE FALSE FALSE

I saved my R code in a script called practice1.R which is stored in the project folder.
First, we load all the packages that we are going to use

library(tidyverse)
library(here)
library(readxl)
library(writexl)

Then, we read the data.

# declare where you are in your project folder
i_am("practice1.R")

# construct the path to your data
path <- here("data", "employees.xlsx")

# read the data and store it in dt
dt <- read_xlsx(path=path)




The function dim() returns the dimensions of the input. The first number is the number of rows. The second denotes the number of columns.

dim(dt)

[1] 150   6


Thus, the dataset stored in dt collects information about 150 employees.
You can extract the same dimensions by using the specialised functions nrow()and ncol()

nrow(dt)

[1] 150

ncol(dt)

[1] 6


A convenient way to quickly summarise the variables in your dataset is the function summary().

summary(dt)

For each variable in your dataset, it returns some summary statistics. In case of numeric values, as for seniority and salary, it provides you with mean and quantiles. mean(dt$seniority)

[1] 7.486667

The exercise asks to construct a scatterplot for salary and seniority, colored by department using the ggplot2 package, which is automatically loaded with tidyverse

salary_plot <- ggplot(dt, aes(x=seniority, y=salary, color=department))+
                    geom_point()
salary_plot








The ggplot2 package offers many options for customising your plots.
A very basic tweak you typically want to apply to your graph is to change its labels by using the labs() function

salary_plot <- salary_plot +
    labs(
        x="Seniority (years since hiring)",
        y="Salary ($)",
        color="Department:"
    )
salary_plot








The labs() function can also be used to set title and subtitle of the plot

salary_plot <- salary_plot +
    labs(
        title="Does salary increase with seniority?",
        subtitle="Department by department evaluation"
    )
salary_plot








When you compare across many groups, it might be more convenient to plot groups in separate panels. You produce such plots by using the facet_grid() or the facet_wrap() functions:

salary_plot+
    facet_grid(~department)









salary_plot <- salary_plot+
    facet_wrap(~department)
salary_plot








You can use preset themes to quickly modify the appearances of your plot. For example

salary_plot + theme_bw()









salary_plot + theme_light()









salary_plot <- salary_plot + theme_minimal()
salary_plot








You can further customise your plot by using the theme() function. See ?theme() for the full list of options available. For example

salary_plot +
    theme(
        legend.position="bottom",        # move the legend in a different position
        panel.grid.minor=element_blank() # remove minor grid lines
    )








Since we are using panels to differentiate across departments, the legend for colors is not really needed, thus, it might be sensible to remove it

salary_plot <- salary_plot +
    theme(
        legend.position="none",  # remove the legend
        panel.grid.minor=element_blank() # declutter the plot by removing minor grid lines
    )
salary_plot








You can also customise the colors of the plots. For example, you can use a customised palette by specifying colors via hex codes,

my_palette <- c(
    "Accounting" = "#F7B1AB",
    "Finance"    = "#807182",
    "HR"         = "#E3DDDD",
    "I.T"        = "#A45C3D",
    "Sales"      = "#5c3410ff",
    "Marketing"  = "#1C0221"
    )
salary_plot +
    scale_color_manual(values=my_palette)








You can use ready-to-use color palettes provided by ggplot2

salary_plot+
    scale_color_viridis_d()








You can also use color palettes provided by external packages, such as ggsci or ggokabeito

library(ggokabeito)
salary_plot <- salary_plot +
    scale_color_okabe_ito()
salary_plot








Nevertheless, there are many other possibilities of customisation. You can find a whole book in this regard in the resources page.
When you are satisfied with your plot, you can save it with the ggsave() function. See ?ggsave() for a list of the exportable formats.

# You can save it in many different formats
ggsave(salary_plot, path = here("salary_plot.jpg")) # save it in jpg format
ggsave(salary_plot, path = here("salary_plot.pdf")) # save it in pdf format
ggsave(salary_plot, path = here("salary_plot.png")) # save it in png format

# You can also customise dimensions to better fit in your documents/slides
ggsave(salary_plot, path = here("salary_plot_wide.jpg"), width=10, height = 5)
ggsave(salary_plot, path = here("salary_plot_square.jpg"), width=8,  height = 8)

title: Data manipulation
text:
Work inside an R Project
Before reading any data, organise your work in an RStudio Project: a folder that contains your scripts and your data.

File -> New Project ... in RStudio creates the project folder.
Move your data file (e.g. employees.xlsx) inside that folder.


The here package builds file paths relative to the project root, so you never hard-code absolute paths like C:/Users/... and never need setwd(). The same code then runs on any machine or collaborator’s laptop:

library(here)

i_am("practice1.R")               # declare where this script lives
path <- here("data", "employees.xlsx")  # build the path to the data
path


i_am() tells here which file you’re running, so it can locate the root.
here("data", "employees.xlsx") then always points to <project>/data/employees.xlsx.

title: Data manipulation
text:
Reading Excel files: read_xlsx()
Proprietary spreadsheets (.xls, .xlsx) need the readxl package:

library(readxl)

path <- here("data", "employees.xlsx")
dt <- read_xlsx(path = path)


An Excel file can contain several sheets. Pick one with the sheet argument:

data <- read_xlsx(path = my_path, sheet = "sheet_name")

title: Data manipulation
text:
Save your results
Use here() to write files into your project too. Take a result like:

my_res <- penguins |>
    group_by(species) |>
    summarise(average_bill_length = mean(bill_length_mm, na.rm = TRUE))
my_res

# A tibble: 3 × 2
  species   average_bill_length
  <fct>                   <dbl>
1 Adelie                   38.8
2 Chinstrap                48.8
3 Gentoo                   47.5


As an R data object:

save(my_res, file = here("my_results.rda"))  # save
load(here("my_results.rda"))                 # load next time

As an Excel file:

library(writexl)
write_xlsx(my_res, path = here("my_results.xlsx"))

text:
Inconsistent column names
Real files rarely have tidy names: spaces, random capitalisation, dots…

raw <- data.frame(`Last NAME` = c("Curie", "Franklin"),
                  `First-name` = c("Marie", "Rosalind"),
                  `Seniority` = c(12, 7),
                  check.names = FALSE)  # keep the messy names as-is

  Last NAME First-name Seniority
1     Curie      Marie        12
2  Franklin   Rosalind         7



clean_names() from the janitor package standardises them to snake_case:

library(janitor)
clean_names(raw)

1     Curie      Marie        12
2  Franklin   Rosalind         7

title: Data manipulation
text:
Missing values
Missing entries are stored as NA. summary() reports them column by column:

my_df

  id ad_type n_clicks sales
1  1  pop-up       56     7
2  2  banner       23    NA
3  3   video      321    25
4  4  banner       NA    10
5  5  pop-up       10    23



Locate them with is.na():

is.na(my_df$n_clicks)

[1] FALSE FALSE FALSE  TRUE FALSE

title: Data manipulation
text:
Missing values: imputation
A common fix is to replace missing values with a summary of the column, e.g. its median. With the tidyverse, combine mutate() and replace():

my_df |>
  mutate(n_clicks = replace(n_clicks, is.na(n_clicks),
                            median(n_clicks, na.rm = TRUE)))

  id ad_type n_clicks sales
1  1  pop-up     56.0     7
2  2  banner     23.0    NA
3  3   video    321.0    25
4  4  banner     39.5    10
5  5  pop-up     10.0    23



Remember: any operation involving NA returns NA, so always pass na.rm = TRUE to the summary function.

The data analysis life cycle







Practice 1: R basics

Exercise 1Exercise 2Exercise 3Exercise 4Exercise 5Exercise 6Exercise 7Exercise 8Exercise 9Exercise 10


Vectors and arithmetic
Imagine you work for a small retail company. You have the prices and quantities sold for 5 products:

prices     <- c(12.5, 8.0, 23.99, 5.50, 15.0)
quantities <- c(3, 10, 1, 25, 7)


Compute the total revenue across all products: use sum(prices * quantities).
How many products are there? Use length(prices).
What’s the most expensive product? Use max(prices).
What’s the cheapest? Use min(prices).
What is prices[3]? What is prices[c(1, 4)]?
Use seq() to create a vector of discount percentages from 5% to 50% in steps of 5%.



Missing values and help
You have monthly sales data, but two months are missing:

monthly_sales <- c(120, 95, NA, 210, NA, 180)


Try mean(monthly_sales). What happens?
Use ?mean to find the argument that ignores missing values. Compute the mean without NAs.
How many values are missing? Use is.na() and sum().
Use ?max. Compute the maximum sale ignoring NAs.
Run ?seq. What does the length.out argument do? Use it to create a vector of 7 evenly spaced values between 0 and 1.



Data frames
Build a data frame from the vectors you created in Exercise 1:

products <- data.frame(
  name     = c("Pen", "Notebook", "Backpack", "Eraser", "Marker"),
  price    = prices,
  quantity = quantities
)


Use dim(products). How many rows and columns?
Use colnames(products) and str(products) to inspect the data frame.
Access the price column with products$price.
Access the 3rd row with products[3, ].
What element is in row 2, column 3?
Use summary(products). What’s the average price?
Show only products with quantity > 5: use products[products$quantity > 5, ].



Fix the code
Each code snippet below contains a mistake. Copy it, run it, read the error message, then fix it.

my_vec <- c(1, 2, 3


maen(my_vec)


My_Vec


matrix(1:6, nrow = 2, ncol = 4)



Logical values and comparisons
You recorded daily temperatures for a week:

temps <- c(18, 22, 25, 30, 28, 35, 20)


Which days were above 25°C? Use temps > 25. What type of object is the result?
How many days were above 25°C? Use sum() on the logical vector.
Use which(temps > 25) to get the positions of the hot days.
Which days were between 20 and 30 (inclusive)? Combine conditions with &: temps >= 20 & temps <= 30.
Were there any days below 15 or above 34? Use |.



Factors
A survey records education levels:

edu <- c("high school", "bachelor", "master", "bachelor", "high school", "PhD", "master")


Convert edu to a factor with as.factor(edu). How does it print differently from the original vector?
Use levels() and nlevels() to inspect the factor.
Now create an ordered factor with factor(), specifying levels = c("high school", "bachelor", "master", "PhD") and ordered = TRUE.
Run sort() on the original character vector and on the ordered factor. What is the difference?
Use table(edu) to count how many respondents fall in each category.



Sequences and repetitions

Use seq(0, 1, by = 0.1) to create a vector from 0 to 1 in steps of 0.1. How many elements does it have?
Use seq(0, 100, length.out = 5) to create exactly 5 evenly spaced values between 0 and 100.
Use rep("A", times = 4) to repeat "A" four times.
Use rep(c("A", "B"), times = 3) and rep(c("A", "B"), each = 3). What is the difference?
Combine: create a vector with the numbers 1 to 3 repeated 4 times each, followed by the value 99. Use c(), rep(), and a scalar.



Matrices
Build a 3x4 matrix of the numbers 1 to 12:

m <- matrix(1:12, nrow = 3, ncol = 4)


Print m. Does R fill the matrix by columns or by rows?
Use nrow(m), ncol(m), and dim(m).
Extract the element in row 2, column 3. Extract the entire second row. Extract the entire fourth column.
Use colSums(m) and rowSums(m). Verify one result by hand.
Try matrix(1:12, nrow = 3, ncol = 4, byrow = TRUE). What changes?



Lists
Create a list that stores information about a student:

student <- list(
  name   = "Alice",
  grades = c(28, 30, 25, 27),
  passed = TRUE
)


Print student. How does it differ from a vector?
Access the name with student$name and with student[["name"]].
Compute the average grade: mean(student$grades).
Use names(student) and length(student).
Add a new element: student$university <- "Milano". Print the list again.



Putting it all together
Build a small dataset about 5 cities:

cities <- data.frame(
  name       = c("Milan", "Rome", "Naples", "Turin", "Bologna"),
  population = c(1396000, 2873000, 967000, 886000, 395000),
  north      = c(TRUE, FALSE, FALSE, TRUE, TRUE)
)


Inspect the data frame with str() and summary().
Show only northern cities: cities[cities$north == TRUE, ].
Add a new column density that equals population / 100 (a made-up simplification). Use cities$density <- ....
Which city has the highest population? Use which.max(cities$population) to get its row index, then extract the city name.
Sort the data frame by population in decreasing order: cities[order(cities$population, decreasing = TRUE), ].






Practice 2: Visualisation with txhousing
The txhousing dataset is included in the tidyverse. Load it with:

library(tidyverse)

Then type txhousing to see it. It contains monthly housing sales data for 46 Texas cities (2000–2015).

Exercise 1Exercise 2Exercise 3Exercise 4Exercise 5Exercise 6Exercise 7Exercise 8Exercise 9Exercise 10


Explore the data

Run head(txhousing) and str(txhousing).
How many observations are there? Use dim().
Run summary(txhousing). What is the range of median house prices? Are there missing values?
Compute the average median house price with mean(). Remember na.rm!



Your first scatterplot

Build a scatterplot of sales (y-axis) vs listings (x-axis):


ggplot(data = txhousing, aes(x = listings, y = sales)) +
  geom_point()


Add labels with labs():

x-axis: "Active listings"
y-axis: "Number of sales"
title: "Texas housing market"

Apply theme_minimal().
Store the final plot in an object called my_plot.



Distributions

Build a histogram of median (median house price):


ggplot(data = txhousing, aes(x = median)) +
  geom_histogram()

Try bins = 10, bins = 30, and bins = 100. What happens with very few vs very many bins?

Build a bar chart showing how many records there are per year:


ggplot(data = txhousing, aes(x = year)) +
  geom_bar()


Add labs() to both plots.



Comparing across groups

Build a boxplot of median house price by month:


ggplot(data = txhousing, aes(x = factor(month), y = median)) +
  geom_boxplot()

Which month has the highest median prices? The most spread?

Build a boxplot of sales by month. Is there a seasonal pattern?
Use ?geom_boxplot. Can you find an argument to change the fill color of the boxes? Try it!
Add labs() and theme_minimal().



Color and facets

Build a scatterplot of volume (y) vs sales (x), colored by year:


ggplot(data = txhousing, aes(x = sales, y = volume, color = year)) +
  geom_point()


What trend do you see?
Add facet_wrap(~month). Does the pattern change across months?
Add labels and a theme.



Numeric vs factor color

Build a scatterplot of listings vs sales, coloring points by month:


ggplot(data = txhousing, aes(x = listings, y = sales, color = month)) +
  geom_point()

What kind of color scale do you get (continuous gradient or discrete palette)?

Now convert month to a factor inside the aes():


ggplot(data = txhousing, aes(x = listings, y = sales, color = factor(month))) +
  geom_point()

How does the legend change? Which version is more informative for this variable?

Add labs(color = "Month") and theme_minimal() to the second version.



Subsetting before plotting

Create a subset of txhousing containing only Houston, Dallas and Austin:


three_cities <- txhousing[txhousing$city %in% c("Houston", "Dallas", "Austin"), ]


How many rows does three_cities have? Use dim().
Build a scatterplot of listings vs sales using three_cities, colored by city:


ggplot(data = three_cities, aes(x = listings, y = sales, color = city)) +
  geom_point()


Add facet_wrap(~city) to separate each city into its own panel. Add labels and a theme.
Try adding San Antonio to the subset and re-run the plot. Does the pattern change?



Creating new variables and plotting

Compute the average price per sale and add it as a new column:


txhousing$price_per_sale <- txhousing$volume / txhousing$sales


Check the result: head(txhousing$price_per_sale). Are there NAs? Why?
Build a histogram of price_per_sale:


ggplot(data = txhousing, aes(x = price_per_sale)) +
  geom_histogram(bins = 40)


Build a boxplot of price_per_sale by year. Use factor(year) on the x-axis so each year gets its own box. Is the average price per sale increasing over time?
Add appropriate labels and theme_minimal().



Combining logical filters with ggplot

Create a logical vector that identifies summer 2010+ observations:


is_summer_recent <- txhousing$year >= 2010 & txhousing$month %in% c(6, 7, 8)


How many TRUE values are there? Use sum().
Subset the data: summer_recent <- txhousing[is_summer_recent, ].
Build a scatterplot of median (y) vs listings (x), colored by factor(year):


ggplot(data = summer_recent, aes(x = listings, y = median, color = factor(year))) +
  geom_point()


Add facet_wrap(~month) to separate June, July, and August. Add labels and a theme.



Changing color palettes
Start from the scatterplot of Exercise 6 with discrete month colors:

ggplot(data = txhousing, aes(x = listings, y = sales, color = factor(month))) +
  geom_point()


Apply a ready-made palette with scale_color_brewer(palette = "Set3"). Try also "Paired" and "Dark2". Which one do you find most readable?
Now use a manual palette. Define your own vector of 12 colors (one per month) and apply it:


my_colors <- c("Jan" = "#1f77b4", "Feb" = "#ff7f0e", "Mar" = "#2ca02c",
                "Apr" = "#d62728", "May" = "#9467bd", "Jun" = "#8c564b",
                "Jul" = "#e377c2", "Aug" = "#7f7f7f", "Sep" = "#bcbd22",
                "Oct" = "#17becf", "Nov" = "#aec7e8", "Dec" = "#ffbb78")

To use named colors you first need to label the months. Create a labeled factor:

txhousing$month_name <- factor(txhousing$month,
                               levels = 1:12,
                               labels = c("Jan","Feb","Mar","Apr","May","Jun",
                                          "Jul","Aug","Sep","Oct","Nov","Dec"))

Then plot with color = month_name and add scale_color_manual(values = my_colors).

Try the continuous version: plot color = median (a numeric variable) and apply scale_color_gradient(low = "blue", high = "red"). How does it differ from the discrete palettes?
Add labs() and theme_minimal() to your favourite version.

Practice: the employees report
In Lab 2 you analysed the employees of two companies with R scripts. Now you will turn that analysis into a report: a single .Rmd file that mixes text, code and results, and that you can re-knit whenever the data change.

my_project/
├── my_project.Rproj
├── report.Rmd          <- you will create this now

Go to File > New File > R Markdown…. In the window that opens, choose Document, set the title to “Employees report”, write your name as author, select HTML and click OK. If RStudio asks to install some packages, accept.
RStudio opens an example document. Save it with File > Save as report.Rmd, directly in the project folder (not inside data).
Click Knit. An HTML page with the example content should open, and a report.html file appears next to report.Rmd.
Now look at the example: the YAML header between ---, the text, the grey code chunks. Then delete everything below the first code chunk (the one starting with ```{r setup, include=FALSE}).

Setup.

Add a table of contents to the output by editing the YAML header. Replace the line output: html_document with the following (indentation matters: use 2 spaces per level):

output:
  html_document:
    toc: true

Complete the setup chunk so that it loads the packages, declares where the report is and imports the data. Replace each ___ with the right value:

```{r setup, include=FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(echo = TRUE)

# packages
library(tidyverse)
library(here)
library(readxl)
library(janitor)

# declare where this file is within the project
i_am("___")

# import the data
dt <- read_xlsx(here("___", "___"))
```

Before knitting, run the chunk with the green ▶ button in its top-right corner, then type dt in the console. Do you see the data? Knit only when the chunk works.
The setup chunk has the option include=FALSE. Knit the document: do you see the code or the data anywhere? What does this option do?
Change echo = TRUE into echo = FALSE, message = FALSE in knitr::opts_chunk$set(). You will see the effect in the next exercises: the code of all the following chunks will be hidden.







TipCommon errors when knitting






`path` does not exist: the file is not where you said it is. Check that employees.xlsx is inside the data folder (or in whatever folder matching your here() call), that the name is spelled exactly the same (capital letters matter), and that report.Rmd is in the project folder.
Could not find associated project in working directory: the file name in i_am() does not match the name of your .Rmd, or you are not working inside the R Project.
object 'dt' not found: knitting starts from an empty session and ignores what you ran in the console. Every object the report uses must be created by a chunk in the .Rmd, above the chunk that uses it.
there is no package called ...: install the missing package from the console with install.packages(). Never put install.packages() inside the .Rmd.






Write a section called ## Overview with a short paragraph reporting:

the number of employees in the company,
their average salary,
the number of new hires (employees with seniority equal to 0).

Do not type any number by hand: use inline R code, for example
The company employs `r nrow(dt)` people.

Write a section called ## Salaries by department.

Add a chunk that computes the summary table of Lab 2 (median salary, number of employees and number of new hires by department) and prints it with knitr::kable(). Use the digits and col.names arguments to make it readable.
Add a chunk with the bar plot of the median salary by department. Give it a caption with the chunk option fig.cap:

```{r median-plot, fig.cap="Median salary by department"}
...
```


Below the plot, write a bullet list of key findings.

One item should state which department has the highest median salary, in bold. Compute the name in a chunk and store it in an object (for example top_dept), then use it with inline code.

Open report.html and report_company2.html side by side. You now have two complete reports, one per company, but you only wrote the text once: every number, table and plot was updated by R. That’s why we write reports in R Markdown!



The readers of the company 2 report should know that some salaries were imputed. In report_company2.Rmd, write a section called ## Data quality.

The setup chunk already replaced the missing salaries in dt. To count them, add a new chunk that reads the raw file again into dt2, cleaning the names but without imputing. You don’t need i_am() again: it is already in the setup chunk.


dt2 <- read_xlsx(here("___", "___")) |>
    clean_names()

The text is written in markdown, a simple syntax for formatted text.

Anatomy of an .Rmd file
---

author: "Giuseppe Alfonzetti"
output: html_document

We analyse the salaries of the company employees.


title: Automatic reporting
text:
Knitting

Create a new file: File > New File > R Markdown…
Click Knit (or Ctrl/Cmd + Shift + K).
R runs every chunk from top to bottom, in a new, clean session, and writes an .html file next to the .Rmd.


Consequences:

objects in your environment are not visible to the report: the .Rmd must load packages and read the data itself;
if a chunk throws an error, knitting stops. Run the chunks one by one (green ▶ button) to debug.

title: Automatic reporting
text:
Paths when knitting
When knitting, the working directory is the folder of the .Rmd file. As in Lab 2, use here() to build paths from the project root:

i_am("report.Rmd")

dt <- read_xlsx(here("data", "employees.xlsx"))


The report now knits correctly wherever you save it within the project.

Options go in the chunk header and control what appears in the output:

hide the code, show the results

include=FALSE
run the code, show nothing


message=FALSE, warning=FALSE
hide messages and warnings


fig.width, fig.height, fig.cap
figure size (inches) and caption

text:

Set default options for all chunks once, at the top of the document:
```{r setup, include=FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(echo = FALSE, message = FALSE, warning = FALSE)

library(here)
library(readxl)

i_am("report.Rmd")
dt <- read_xlsx(here("data", "employees.xlsx"))
```

title: Solutions Lab 3 practice
text:
Exercise 1
The YAML header sets the title, author, date and output format. toc: true adds a table of contents, and toc_float: true keeps it visible on the side while you scroll. The date is inline R code, so it updates every time you knit.
---
title: "Employees report"
author: "Write here your name"
output:
  html_document:
    toc: true
    toc_float: true
---
The setup chunk runs all the code the rest of the report needs. With include=FALSE, the chunk is run but neither its code nor its output appears in the report. knitr::opts_chunk$set() sets default options for all the following chunks. Here, echo = FALSE hides the code, because the reader of a report wants results, not R code.
```{r setup, include=FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(echo = FALSE, message = FALSE, warning = FALSE)

library(tidyverse)
library(here)
library(readxl)
library(janitor)

i_am("report.Rmd")

dt <- read_xlsx(here("data", "employees.xlsx"))
```
Recall that when you knit, R starts from a clean session. Objects in your environment are not visible, so everything the report uses must be created inside the .Rmd.

title: Solutions Lab 3 practice
text:
Exercise 2
Every number is computed with inline code:
## Overview

The company employs **`r nrow(dt)`** people.
The average salary is `r format(round(mean(dt$salary)), big.mark = ",")` dollars, and `r sum(dt$seniority == 0)` employees have just been hired.
When printing inline, knitr writes large numbers in scientific notation, so round(mean(dt$salary)) shows up as something like 1.04 × 10⁵. format() with big.mark = "," prints 103,789 instead.

title: Solutions Lab 3 practice
text:
Exercise 3
knitr::kable() turns a data frame into a formatted table. digits rounds numbers and col.names replaces the column names in the output only (the data frame is unchanged).
```{r report-table}
report_table <- dt |>
    group_by(department) |>
    summarise(
        med_sal   = median(salary),
        total_n   = n(),
        new_hires = sum(seniority == 0)
    )

knitr::kable(
    report_table,
    digits    = 0,
    col.names = c("Department", "Median salary", "Employees", "New hires")
)
```

```{r median-plot, fig.cap="Median salary by department"}
ggplot(report_table, aes(x = department, y = med_sal)) +
    geom_col() +
    labs(x = "", y = "Median salary ($)") +
    theme_minimal()
```

title: Solutions Lab 3 practice
text:
Exercise 4
We add the name of the best paid department to the report-table chunk, so that it is available in the text:

top_dept <- report_table |>
    filter(med_sal == max(med_sal)) |>
    pull(department)

pull() extracts a column as a plain vector. Then we write the findings as a markdown bullet list, with the scatterplot in between:
Key findings:

- The best paid department is **`r top_dept`**, with a median salary of `r format(round(max(report_table$med_sal)), big.mark = ",")` dollars.
- The largest department is `r report_table$department[which.max(report_table$total_n)]`, with `r max(report_table$total_n)` employees.
- Salaries grow with seniority in every department:

```{r seniority-plot, fig.cap="Salary and seniority by department"}
ggplot(dt, aes(x = seniority, y = salary, color = department)) +
    geom_point() +
    facet_wrap(~department) +
    labs(x = "Seniority (years since hiring)", y = "Salary ($)") +
    theme_minimal() +
    theme(legend.position = "none")
```

The analysis was carried out with the [tidyverse](https://www.tidyverse.org/).

## Data quality

```{r raw-data}
dt2 <- read_xlsx(here("data", "employees_company2.xlsx")) |>
    clean_names()

n_missing <- sum(is.na(dt2$salary))
```

The original file has `r n_missing` missing salaries.
We replaced each missing salary with the median salary of its department.

```{r imputation-table}
before <- dt2 |>
    group_by(department) |>
    summarise(missing = sum(is.na(salary)), mean_before = mean(salary, na.rm = TRUE))

after <- dt |>
    group_by(department) |>
    summarise(mean_after = mean(salary))

before |>
    left_join(after, by = "department") |>
    knitr::kable(
        digits    = 0,
        col.names = c("Department", "Missing salaries", "Mean before", "Mean after")
    )
```
